newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Ogoni welcome UN naming new rights envoy on Nigeria.
newsitem.headline: Ogoni welcome UN naming new rights envoy on Nigeria.

text.p: The U.N. Human Rights Commission on Tuesday appointed its first special investigator into allegations of major rights abuses in Nigeria, including arbitrary detentions and executions.

In the resolution adopted by the 53-member forum, it also called on the Lagos government to guarantee fundamental freedoms and release "all prisoners, trade union leaders, human rights advocates and journalists currently detained".
The text urges Nigeria to ensure that all trials are held fairly and promptly in conformity with international standards.

The main U.N. human rights forum was widely expected to censure Nigeria at this year's session by naming a specific "country rapporteur" or investigator for Africa's most populous nation and an OPEC member.
The vote was 28 states in favour of the resolution, six states against with 19 abstentions. Nigeria is not a member at this year's Commission, which has a rotating membership.
"It is the first time the Commission has named a special rapporteur for Nigeria," a U.N. source told Reuters. "The strong support from African countries was surprising."

South Africa and Uganda voted for the resolution against Nigeria. The vote was also remarkable for abstentions by 10 African countries -- Algeria, Angola, Cape Verde, Egypt, Ethiopia, Guinea, Madagascar, Mali, Mozambique and Zimbabwe.

Nigeria drew international condemnation in November 1995 when it hanged Saro Wiwa and eight Ogoni minority rights activists after their conviction in the 1994 murder of four pro-government tribal chiefs. Their trial was judged unfair by international judicial experts but they were denied the right to appeal.
In a statement issued in Geneva, the London-based Movement for the Survival of the Ogoni People (MOSOP), welcomed the move.

"The Movement for the Survival of the Ogoni People gives kudos to the members of the U.N. Human Rights Commission for overwhelmingly voting to deplore the gross violations of human rights perpetrated by the General Sani Abacha dictatorship in Nigeria, and in particular, to appoint a country-specific rapporteur to report on all aspects of rights violations in Nigeria," the statement, signed by Barika Idamkue, said.

"The vote is a clear indication that the international community has chosen to pitch its tent with the suffering people of Nigeria, including the peace-loving people of Ogoniland in Nigeria who have been under military siege since the judicial murder of Ken Saro-Wiwa and either other members of MOSOP in November 1995," it added.
Some 19 jailed Ogoni leaders in Port Harcourt, linked to Saro Wiwa, face the death penalty on the same murder charges.

Two "thematic" special U.N. rapporteurs (investigators), those looking into independence of judges and lawyers, and extrajudical or arbitrary executions, called for naming an investigator for Nigeria in their latest report this month.

They called off a mission to Nigeria in Feburary due to a last-minute row with the government over access to detainees, according to the latest report by the rapporteurs, Malaysian lawyer Param Cumaraswamy and Senegal's Bacre Waly Ndiaye.
The government agreed to grant access to the jailed Ogonis, but wanted to deny access to detainees who have already been judged, according to their report.
